strengths: Elegantly reformulates multi-vector MaxSim search into a supervised multi-output regression problem, enabling a natural factorization where query tokens are mapped nonlinearly and pooled, while document representations become learned linear weights, reducing the candidate search directly to single-vector MIPS.

Decoupled training pipeline—pre-training the feature encoder on a document subset followed by per-document closed-form OLS solutions—is computationally practical, enabling fast CPU indexing (>1000 documents/sec) and trivial incremental document indexing.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple diverse multi-vector text models (ColBERTv2, Jina-ColBERT-v2, ModernColBERT, LFM2) and vision-language retrievers (ColQwen2, ModernVBERT) on BEIR and ViDoRe benchmarks, demonstrating broad generalizability.

Significantly outperforms state-of-the-art multi-vector retrieval engines (PLAID, MUVERA, IGP, DESSERT), achieving 5-11x speedups at 80% recall on standard benchmarks while demonstrating superior robustness across model architectures where previous reductions fail.
Well-designed ablation studies investigating the effect of latent dimension size, ANNS indexing vs. exact MIPS, and training data selection (query vs. corpus document representations).
weaknesses: The index memory overhead is not quantitatively contrasted with token-pruned baselines: storing 2048-dimensional dense vectors plus HNSW graphs for large collections (e.g., 8.8M MS MARCO passages) requires substantial RAM, and a detailed memory breakdown against PLAID and MUVERA would clarify the trade-offs.
The paper lacks an end-to-end indexing time comparison (feature encoder pre-training + OLS fitting + ANNS index construction) against competing baselines like PLAID or IGP.

While the paper shows that the feature encoder can be trained on a subset of documents, it does not evaluate how robust the fixed encoder $\psi$ remains under severe out-of-distribution corpus drift where document topics diverge significantly from the pre-training slice.

strengths: Elegant and conceptually clean formulation: Decomposing the MaxSim objective into additive token contributions g_l(x) = \max_{c \in C_l} \langle c, x \rangle and approximating g with a two-layer MLP with a linear head allows query-side pooling \Psi(X) = \sum_{x \in X} \psi(x), cleanly reducing multi-vector candidate search to standard single-vector MIPS.
Strong empirical results: LEMUR consistently outperforms competitive baselines (PLAID, DESSERT, IGP, MUVERA) across multiple datasets, achieving 5-11x speedups at 80% recall on ColBERTv2 embeddings.

Comprehensive benchmarking across modern embedding models: Unlike most prior work which benchmarks exclusively on ColBERTv2, this paper evaluates newer text models (GTE-ModernColBERT, LFM2-ColBERT, Jina-ColBERT-v2) and multimodal visual document models (ColQwen2, ColModernVBERT), demonstrating the robustness and generalizability of the proposed approach.

Thoughtful and scalable training design: Pre-training the token feature encoder \psi on a subset of targets and solving linear regression (OLS) in closed form for document weights enables fast index construction (>1,000 documents/sec) without requiring end-to-end retraining for each new document.
weaknesses: Incomplete quantification of index construction time and memory overhead: While query latency versus recall is thoroughly analyzed, the paper lacks explicit end-to-end comparisons with baselines regarding total index build time and RAM/disk footprint (e.g., storing d'=2048 float/quantized vectors per document alongside the original multi-vector representations for reranking).

Limited theoretical characterization: The function g_l(x) is the upper envelope of |C_l| linear functions (a convex, piece-wise linear function). The paper does not provide theoretical insight or approximation error bounds on representing this family of functions with inner products w_l^T \psi(x) in dimension d'.

Evaluation metric scope: The evaluation strictly measures recall against exact MaxSim (which is standard for ANNS papers in this subfield), but reporting downstream retrieval quality metrics (such as nDCG@10 on BEIR benchmarks) would confirm that the retrieval approximation does not adversely affect end-to-end task effectiveness.

strengths: Elegant and principled problem reduction: Reformulating MaxSim retrieval into a token-level supervised regression problem and exploiting the additive structure of MaxSim to yield a single-vector MIPS problem (via sum-pooling the query token latent representations and inner product with learned document vectors) is both mathematically sound and creative.

Scalable training scheme: The two-stage training approach—pre-training the feature encoder on an auxiliary subset of documents and computing document latent representations independently via closed-form ordinary least squares (OLS)—elegantly sidesteps the computational bottleneck of joint optimization across massive corpora (e.g., 8.8M documents in MS MARCO).

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: The paper evaluates LEMUR against state-of-the-art multi-vector ANNS baselines (MUVERA, IGP, DESSERT, PLAID) across 6 BEIR benchmark datasets, 5 different multi-vector text encoders (ColBERTv2, AnswerAI, GTE-ModernColBERT, Jina, LFM2), and 2 visual document retrieval models on ViDoRe.

Substantial speedup: LEMUR demonstrates compelling Pareto efficiency, delivering a 5x–11x speedup at 80% recall compared to competitive baselines on ColBERTv2, and robustly handles non-ColBERT embedding geometries where baselines like MUVERA degrade.

Seamless integration with modern vector database infrastructure: By reducing multi-vector candidate generation to single-vector MIPS, LEMUR can directly leverage existing highly optimized ANNS libraries (e.g., Glass, HNSW, Faiss).
weaknesses: Omission of index build time and memory footprint comparisons: In ANNS literature, query latency/QPS must be contextualized alongside indexing throughput and RAM/disk overhead. While the authors state that OLS processes ~1,000 documents/second, a complete quantitative comparison of offline index construction time and total storage footprint (latent vectors + graph index + multi-vector token store for reranking) against PLAID, MUVERA, and IGP is missing.

Lack of downstream IR metrics: The evaluation focuses exclusively on Recall@k relative to exact MaxSim. While standard for ANNS system papers, reporting downstream task performance (such as NDCG@10 or MRR@10) across varying candidate set sizes k' would confirm that retrieval quality is fully preserved in practical settings.

High recall plateau and dimensionality trade-offs: At very high recall regimes (recall > 0.95), the benefits of the learned single-vector proxy diminish noticeably, requiring large candidate pools k' where the overhead of the ANNS search plus MaxSim reranking approaches exact search.

Minor presentation flaws: On page 2 (end of column 1), there is a dangling sentence ('The code for LEMUR is available at 
 In summary...'). Even for double-blind submissions, placeholders should be properly formatted rather than left as incomplete sentences.

strengths: Elegantly reformulates multi-vector MaxSim approximation as a multi-output regression problem on token support functions, enabling exact linearity over query token pooling and reducing late-interaction candidate generation directly to standard single-vector MIPS.

Highly scalable training and indexing strategy: pre-training the non-linear feature encoder on an auxiliary document subset and computing document representations via closed-form OLS enables indexing an 8.8M document corpus in a few hours without expensive clustering.
Extensive and rigorous empirical evaluation across eight BEIR datasets and the ViDoRe V3 visual retrieval benchmark, spanning seven diverse multi-vector text and vision models.
Substantial empirical gains: achieves an order-of-magnitude speedup (5-16x higher QPS at >=80% recall) over competitive baselines including PLAID, MUVERA, DESSERT, and IGP.

Thorough ablation and robustness analysis, demonstrating effectiveness across varying latent dimensions, robustness to training data distribution (including corpus-only embeddings and random ELM hidden layers), and long-query retrieval.
weaknesses: The corpus-specific projection matrix requires solving an OLS problem and maintaining a d'=2048 dimensional vector per document, which incurs noticeable index storage and maintenance overhead compared to purely zero-shot or token-clustering indexing methods.

Theoretical analysis (Theorem B.1) is primarily an application of classical universal approximation theorems for MLPs on compact sets, offering asymptotic guarantees without finite-sample error bounds or scaling laws as corpus size m increases.

Evaluations are strictly CPU-based; while the paper notes that both query processing and indexing can be adapted to GPU libraries like CAGRA, empirical validation in GPU-accelerated environments is left unexamined.
The performance advantage over baselines narrows on visual document models (ViDoRe) due to the dominating latency of late-stage reranking on larger patch/image token sequences.

strengths: Elegant theoretical and architectural framing: Decomposing the MaxSim objective into the sum of per-token support functions and approximating them via an MLP with a linear readout naturally reduces multi-vector candidate generation to single-vector MIPS via sum-pooling in the latent space.

Outstanding empirical efficiency gains: Across eight BEIR text benchmarks and the ViDoRe visual document retrieval benchmark, LEMUR consistently outperforms state-of-the-art multi-vector search baselines (PLAID, MUVERA, IGP, DESSERT), achieving 5–16x speedups at >= 80% recall.

Robustness across modern embedding models: Unlike heuristic or data-oblivious reductions (e.g., MUVERA), which suffer significant performance drops on newer architectures such as GTE-ModernColBERT and LFM2-ColBERT, LEMUR demonstrates consistent, high recall and low latency across all tested models.

Efficient and practical indexing: The decoupling into a shared feature encoder and per-document linear regression weights eliminates expensive token-level clustering over hundreds of millions of embeddings, scaling linearly with corpus size and enabling fast CPU-based indexing.

Thorough ablation and analysis: The paper includes insightful experiments regarding latent dimensionality, correlation with exact MaxSim scores, query length scaling (ArguAna), training set selection (queries vs. corpus vs. document encoder), and extreme learning machine (random feature) baselines.
weaknesses: Memory footprint and storage analysis could be more comprehensive: Although LEMUR's latent dimension (d' = 2048) is substantially smaller than MUVERA's (10240-d FDEs), storing a 2048-dimensional vector per document along with the HNSW graph index still represents a non-trivial memory overhead on top of the original multi-vector corpus. A clear table detailing the index sizes and RAM consumption compared to PLAID and other baselines would clarify operational trade-offs.

Evaluation is restricted to CPU environments: While the authors note that both indexing and querying can be ported to GPUs (e.g., via CAGRA), experimental verification of GPU throughput and latency would provide a more complete assessment for modern dense retrieval serving infrastructure.

Sensitivity to auxiliary sample size m': While the choice of m' = 8192 documents for pretraining the encoder works well across datasets, the paper does not provide an ablation on how varying m' affects the quality of the feature map.

strengths: Conceptual elegance: Framing the multi-vector MaxSim search as a supervised multi-output regression over document support functions ($g_l(x) = \max_{c \in C_l} \langle x, c \rangle$), combined with a linear output layer, provides an exceptionally clean reduction to single-vector MIPS without needing heuristic token clustering.

Practicality and indexing efficiency: Pretraining the hidden layer feature encoder $\psi$ on a small subset of documents and computing document representations $w_j$ via closed-form OLS makes indexing highly scalable, parallelizable, and capable of incremental updates without costly token-level re-clustering.

Comprehensive and rigorous evaluation: The method is tested across 8 BEIR text datasets and the ViDoRe V3 multimodal benchmark, covering 5 distinct multi-vector text encoders and 2 visual document retrieval models, where it consistently outperforms PLAID, DESSERT, IGP, and MUVERA.

Thorough ablations: The authors provide detailed empirical analyses covering latent dimension sensitivity, rank correlation with exact MaxSim, long-query performance (ArguAna), extreme learning machine (ELM) with fixed random features, and various training data sampling regimes.
High clarity and presentation quality: The paper is lucidly written, theoretically grounded with universal approximation framing, and easy to follow.
weaknesses: Memory footprint details: While LEMUR operates at a lower embedding dimension ($d'=2048$) than MUVERA ($10240$), maintaining a 2048-dimensional HNSW index alongside raw token multi-vectors for candidate reranking carries a noticeable RAM requirement; an explicit tabular memory footprint comparison against baselines like PLAID or compressed multi-vector stores would strengthen the analysis.

Corpus-specific OLS overhead: Although solving OLS for incoming documents is much faster than re-clustering billions of tokens, incremental updates still require computing and storing projection vectors against the cached pseudo-inverse matrix $Z^+$, which may introduce engineering friction in strictly dynamic, streaming environments.
